title: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters
learningObjectives: Define an MCI by the resource gap, not by a casualty number.
Classify incidents: open vs closed, simple vs compound, compensated vs uncompensated.
Classify disasters (natural vs human-made) and predict the dominant injury pattern of each.
Explain the mindset shift from 'best care for one' to 'most good for the most'.

summary.title: What Makes It an MCI
summary.content: An MCI is any incident where the number or severity of casualties exceeds the resources immediately available. Three patients on a rural road with one ambulance can be an MCI; 15 patients downtown with 20 units nearby may not be. Local plans set activation tiers (e.g., Level 1/2/3 by patient count) — know yours, but the definition is always the resource gap. A disaster is an MCI that overwhelms the whole community's response capacity and needs outside help.

summary.title: The Mindset Shift
summary.content: Daily EMS = maximum care for each patient. MCI = the greatest good for the greatest number. You triage, do seconds-long lifesaving interventions, and move on. CPR on an arrested patient, full spinal packaging, and detailed exams are luxuries the scene can't afford until resources catch up.

summary.title: Classify the Incident in One Line
summary.content: CLOSED (contained) — finite, known number of victims, e.g., a bus crash. OPEN (uncontained) — victims keep appearing or the number is unknown, e.g., earthquake, ongoing shooter, toxic plume. SIMPLE — infrastructure intact (roads, hospitals, comms work). COMPOUND — infrastructure itself is damaged (hospital flooded, roads cut, cell network down). COMPENSATED — the system can absorb it with extra resources. UNCOMPENSATED — it can't, even with mutual aid → disaster. Open + compound is the worst case: expect long scene times and self-sufficiency.

summary.title: Types of Disasters
summary.content: NATURAL: geophysical (earthquake, tsunami, volcano, landslide), hydrological (flood), meteorological (hurricane/cyclone, tornado, blizzard), climatological (heat wave, wildfire, drought), biological (pandemic, epidemic). HUMAN-MADE: technological/industrial (HazMat release, explosion, structural collapse, utility failure), transportation (bus, rail, air, maritime), intentional (terrorism/CBRNE, active shooter, vehicle ramming, armed conflict), and mass-gathering/crowd events (crowd crush, stampede). Tactically: the disaster TYPE predicts the INJURY pattern, the HAZARDS to you, and whether infrastructure is intact.

summary.title: The Disaster Cycle (One Paragraph)
summary.content: Mitigation (reduce risk) → Preparedness (plans, drills, caches, training) → Response (the incident) → Recovery (restore services, debrief, rebuild) → back to mitigation. EMS lives in response, but MCIs are won in preparedness: knowing your MCI plan, your role cards, and where the triage tags are BEFORE the call.

clinicalPearls: MCI is a math problem: patients > resources. Declare it early — standing down an over-call is cheap; catching up an under-call is not.

Disaster type → injury pattern: earthquake = crush; flood = drowning/hypothermia/trauma from debris; tornado = penetrating debris + blunt; blast = blast lung + fragments; crowd crush = compressive asphyxia.
In an OPEN incident, never assume the patient count you were dispatched to is the final count.
Compound incidents (infrastructure damaged) mean plan for long holds on scene and limited hospital capacity.
Hurricanes and ice storms kill AFTER the event too: CO poisoning from generators, falls during cleanup, chainsaw injuries, missed dialysis and oxygen.
redFlags: Waiting for a 'certain number' of patients before declaring an MCI.
Treating the first critical patient you find and losing the scene.
Assuming hospitals and roads are working in a regional disaster.
Repeated incidents or a second explosion — consider an intentional event with secondary devices.
commonMistakes: Defining MCI by a fixed number rather than the resource gap.
Confusing closed (finite victims) with open (ongoing/unknown victims).
Forgetting the 'after-disaster' injury wave (CO, cleanup trauma, chronic disease decompensation).
memoryAids: MCI = Patients > Resources. Disaster = Community > Capacity.
Open/Closed = how many victims. Simple/Compound = is infrastructure intact.
N-H split: Natural (Geo-Hydro-Meteo-Climato-Bio) vs Human-made (Tech, Transport, Terror, Crowds).

decisionTrees.title: Is This an MCI?
decisionTrees.content:
Arrive / receive report
  → Casualties (number × severity) > resources immediately available?
     → NO: routine operations, but re-assess as info arrives
     → YES: DECLARE MCI
        → Closed or open? (finite vs ongoing/unknown victims)
        → Simple or compound? (infrastructure intact?)
        → Hazards? (CBRNE, structural, violence)
        → Send METHANE report and activate MCI plan / request resources

references: WHO / CRED disaster classification (natural hazard groups)
